items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
items.summary: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
items.summary: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

items.title: Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs
items.summary: This post walks developers through training a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix and Gemma 4 on Cloud TPUs. By leveraging agentic Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and asynchronous vLLM rollouts, the approach significantly improves complex reasoning and tool compliance in interactive environments.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
items.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
items.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. A typical client-side grader looks something like this: export function grade(attempt, bank) { let score = 0; for (const q of attempt.answers) { const item = bank[q.id]; if (normalize(q.value) === item.correct) score += item.weight; } return { score, passed: score >= bank.passMark }; } After a production build, bank is either inlined in a chunk or fetched from /questions.json. Either way it contains every question, every correct field, the weights, the pass mark, and frequently the question pool you meant to rotate over the next three cohorts. The same code run on a machine in Taipei and on a host whose time zone is set to UTC writes values 8 hours apart, and nothing in the table shows the difference. Retries then repeat delivery attempts without repeating the business effect. This is a delivery-guarantee problem, not a queue-selection slogan. A worker can finish sending a digest and disappear before its acknowledgement reaches the broker. The next delivery is expected. The dangerous design is the one that treats the second delivery as exceptional and has no durable record with which to decide what happened. A logistics digest might summarize shipments active at the end of a week: delayed consignments, customs holds, and parcels awaiting handoff. The producer should create one command for the intended recipient and period, for example digest:customer-1842:2026-W32, and carry that key through every retry. A queue delivery identifier is not suitable for this job because a redelivery normally receives a new identifier while the customer-period intent remains the same. items.title: How a web page can measure your mouse's polling rate
items.summary: Gaming mice advertise 1000, 4000, even 8000 Hz: how often the mouse reports its position to the PC. But is yours actually running at that rate? They bundle all the moves since the last frame into one event, so you'd measure your screen's refresh rate, not your mouse. items.title: Missing frame-src in CSP Blocks YouTube, Kills Watch Logs
items.summary: Conclusion Without a frame-src directive in the CSP, default-src 'self' blocks the iframe embed itself, so no YouTube video plays at all — even with script-src allowing the YouTube domain. And if script-src doesn't allow that domain either, the IFrame Player API script can't load, so window.YT — which the player depends on — never gets defined. That means playback isn't the only thing that breaks: the watch-time logging that monitors playback state and reports it also stops, silently. The fix was adding the exact domains YouTube actually uses to three separate directives: script-src, img-src, and frame-src. The CSP for a learning-video platform was defined in one place, securityHeaders in next.config.ts. Before the fix it looked like this: const securityHeaders = [ // ... { key: 'Content-Security-Policy', value: [ "default-src 'self'", "script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'", "style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'", `connect-src 'self' https://*.supabase.co wss://*.supabase.co`, "img-src 'self' data:", "font-src 'self'", "frame-ancestors 'none'", ].join('; '), }, ] There is no frame-src directive at all. The classic WordPress setup PHP on shared hosting or managed WordPress platforms, coupled with a MySQL database and a plugin ecosystem works reliably but comes with inherent performance trade-offs. Modern visitors now expect lightning-fast page loads and perfect Core Web Vitals a bar that traditional WordPress setups struggle to meet without extensive optimization and caching strategies. Astro is a modern web framework that prioritizes delivering fast, lightweight content by default. items.summary: Refactoring Anxiety: 5 Cognitive Distortions That Sabotage Your Code Cleanup You stare at the legacy module. You know it needs refactoring. The tech debt is piling up, the bug reports are mounting, and every new feature takes twice as long as it should. But you can't bring yourself to touch it. "What if I break something?" you think. "What if I make it worse? Maybe I'm not smart enough to understand this code. Maybe I should just rewrite it from scratch." If this sounds familiar, you're not dealing with a technical problem — you're dealing with refactoring anxiety, a specific form of cognitive distortion that hits developers when facing legacy code. Refactoring anxiety is the irrational fear that arises when a developer considers modifying existing code that "works but is a mess." It's not about the code itself — it's about the thoughts and beliefs you attach to the code. In Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), we learn that thoughts create feelings, not situations. items.title: Why Image Compressors Strip Metadata — and How to Prevent It
items.summary: If you have ever run images through a compression pipeline and discovered the EXIF data came out empty, the explanation is usually straightforward: the compressor never handled the metadata in the first place. Image compression operates on pixel data. Metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS coordinates — is stored in structurally separate sections of the file. Whether those sections survive compression is entirely a function of how the tool is built. JPEG files use marker segments to organize data. The pixel stream starts at the SOS (Start of Scan) marker. Metadata lives in application markers: APP1 (0xFFE1) — EXIF and XMP payloads APP13 (0xFFED) — IPTC-IIM data APP2 (0xFFE2) — ICC color profiles Low-level libraries like libjpeg and libjpeg-turbo process only the pixel buffer. They do not automatically parse or carry over APPn markers. To preserve metadata, the developer must explicitly intercept markers during reading (via jpeg_save_markers()) and reinject them during writing (via jpeg_write_marker()). items.title: React y CSS: una frontera de email accesible
items.summary: Un campo de email parece pequeño, pero suele ser la frontera entre una interfaz amable y un flujo dificil de entender. El navegador conoce el valor escrito, el backend conoce la respuesta de verificación y la persona usuaria solo ve cambios de color, mensajes y botones que se habilitan o no. Cuando cada capa decide por su cuenta, aparecen estados contradictorios: el input dice “válido”, el botón muestra un spinner y el servidor responde que el enlace expiró. La solución que me resulta más estable es tratar esa frontera como un componente explícito de React. Así se puede medir el tiempo de cada transición, revisar su accesibilidad y probarla sin depender de una bandeja personal. Antes de escribir JSX, define qué significa cada estado. Una lista corta suele ser suficiente: idle: todavía no hay una decisión que comunicar. checking: el formato local pasó y se consulta al backend. accepted: el email puede continuar al siguiente paso. invalid: hay una corrección concreta que hacer. expired: el enlace o el mensaje ya no sirve y toca solicitar otro. El error frecuente es mezclar “el formato parece correcto” con “la verificación terminó”. Son hechos diferentes y merecen mensajes diferentes.

items.title: Trump Vows To Stop US Companies From Building Data Centers Abroad
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from CNBC: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy -- which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Node.js Background Job Queue — Create an Idempotent Reconciliation Worker
items.summary: Create a Node.js background job queue with one idempotent worker when a nightly payment reconciliation can be split into independent jobs. Short answer: let the queue provide at-least-once delivery, while the application owns duplicate suppression, consume-and-ack behavior, retry policy, and dead-letter recovery. Choose a workflow engine instead when correctness depends on a durable sequence, fan-out join, or long-running coordination. This decision optimizes operational recovery, not feature count. The non-negotiable invariants are small messages, a durable idempotency record, acknowledgement only after the business result commits, and a dead-letter queue that an operator can inspect and redrive. For a logistics system, a message should carry a reconciliation job identifier or payment-provider reference, not an entire shipment ledger, and must remain below 256KB. The queue owns delivery. items.title: State in enterprise frontends: ownership before libraries
items.summary: This is part 2 of 8 of the free series Frontend system design for enterprise applications, first published on tt-tech.io. A support agent opens the link a customer sent: an account page, filtered on one category. The page shows all categories, because the filter lived in a component field and not in the URL. Nobody wrote a bug. The state was stored as the wrong kind. That is the state problem in enterprise apps. The library choice comes last. First you decide what kind each piece of state is, who owns it, and how long it lives. Server data. Accounts, transactions. The backend owns it; the frontend holds a copy that can be stale (part 3). UI state. Which panel is open. Owned by one component, gone when it is gone. Form state. A draft, its validation, whether it is dirty. URL state. Filters, tabs, the selected record. Anything a link, a support ticket or the back button must restore. Session state. The user and their roles. Truly global. A common state bug is one kind stored as another: server data copied into a component, a filter in memory that belongs in the URL, roles cached in a store nobody refreshes. NBC News reports: The S&P 500 was trading nearly 2% lower as it headed for its worst losing week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced his "Liberation Day" tariffs, and is now 10% off from its most recent high, entering what's known as "correction territory." Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026. Other major AI-related names such as CoreWeave, Nvidia and Oracle also sold off. The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index's longest losing streak since April 2024. A seventh losing day would make it the longest stretch since the pandemic slump in February 2020, according to Deutsche Bank. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Building a transit map editor in the browser: 45 routing, rounded corners and parallel line bundling
items.summary: Microsoft Publisher is being discontinued at the end of October 2026. For years I used it for a hobby: designing transit network maps, the kind with colored lines, 45° bends and round stop symbols. I don’t need InDesign for that, and I couldn’t find a simple replacement. So I built one. It’s called Liniennetz-Editor, it’s free and open source (MIT), and it runs completely in the browser with no backend. Here’s how it works and what turned out to be tricky. Graphics programs make you draw every line segment. For a network with 50 lines and 300 stations that is miserable. The editor flips this around: Describe the network: stops, lines, categories (e.g. “frequent” vs. “rare”), which line serves which stops Place the stops on a grid The program computes everything else: connections, corners, parallel lanes, stop symbols, key The result is a modern-looking map that only uses 0°, 45° and 90°, exported as SVG, PNG or PDF. items.title: Cloud Storage for Storing User Uploads in Node.js — Edtech Restore Integrity
items.summary: Short answer: choose the object store that fits your existing identity, deployment, and data-residency controls, then make restore integrity the application contract. For an edtech platform storing user documents, the important comparison is not which service can accept an upload. All three can do that. The useful question is whether a Node.js backup pipeline can prove that a selected tenant snapshot is complete, unchanged, and safe to restore. That shifts the decision axis from delivery convenience to recovery evidence. Keep the manifest in a database, keep the document bytes in object storage, and make every restore verify the relationship between them. A five-minute signed request can move bytes; it cannot prove that the manifest and the bytes belong to the same backup. The bytes are only half the backup. items.title: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
items.summary: Hi HN! Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer. OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure). We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]). Two other choices: - One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM. We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient. Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3]. [1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev Comments URL: https://news

items.summary: Photo by cottonbro studio on Pexels I'm Samson Sunny, the developer behind Wednesday Calendar, a daily planning app built around a simple idea: Today should mean today. Last week I shipped something I did not expect to enjoy this much: a development agent that takes instructions from my email inbox, implements them in the main checkout, runs the Xcode build, pushes to main, and emails me back with the result. No dashboard. No ticket board. No custom web app. Just an email that looks like this: Subject: [dev] Fix Today badge count Completed tasks should not count toward the Today badge. Update the view model and run the build. A minute later I get a reply: Request: [dev] Fix Today badge count Target: main Build: passed Commit: 7ca1230 Pushed: origin/main Agent summary: Updated TodayViewModel so badge counts exclude completed tasks... That is the whole interface. It turns out email is a surprisingly good agent control surface. Every other automation interface I considered asked me to change how I work. Email did not. items.title: I built an ML signal platform for the Colombo Stock Exchange. The model was the easy part.
items.summary: Most "AI trading bot" posts show a chart that goes up and to the right. This is not one of those. Over the last few months I built a full machine-learning research and signal platform for the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in Sri Lanka, as a solo personal project. It collects the data, cleans it, trains and tests models, and turns the result into clear daily guidance in a web dashboard. It does not trade by itself: every order is still placed by a person. The biggest lesson? Building the model took maybe 20% of the time. Data, honest testing and guardrails took the rest. Here is how it is put together and what I learned. Why a small market is hard (and interesting) The CSE is not the NYSE. A few things make it tricky: Thin liquidity. Many listed shares trade only a few times a day. A model that loves an illiquid stock is useless if you cannot actually buy it. That shaped every design decision. The data pipeline The first job was getting 15+ years of daily prices for 700+ securities: more than 1 million rows. items.title: 5 Security Mistakes I See in Flask + React Apps (and How to Fix Them)
items.summary: Flask and React are a great pairing: fast to build, flexible, and easy to deploy. But that same speed means security often gets pushed to "later," and later usually means after something breaks. I work as a secure software engineer, and these five mistakes keep showing up in tutorials, side projects, and early-stage apps. None of them are exotic. All of them are fixable in a few lines. 1. Trusting user input without validation The mistake: Reading values straight from request.get_json() and using them as if they were safe and correctly shaped. python # ❌ Before @app.route("/register", methods=["POST"]) def register(): data = request.get_json() email = data["email"] # KeyError if missing, anything if present password = data["password"] # no length or type checks create_user(email, password) return {"message": "ok"}, 201 Missing fields crash the endpoint, and unexpected types or oversized strings flow deeper into your app. The fix: Validate every request body against a schema before touching it. Pydantic works well for this (pip install pydantic email-validator). python # ✅ After from flask import request, jsonify from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, ValidationError class

The broker connection, retries and duplicate protection, database migrations, deployment, monitoring. In the estimate it hides under "architecture" and "integration", and the client still asks why it takes so long. I have been building backends for clients for over twenty years, and for the last three years and more I have built them on my own open source .NET ecosystem, redb. This article is about why it is a convenient stack for a firm that builds software for clients: what gets faster, what is easier to hand over, and where its honest limits are. The ecosystem is a data store, the redb.Route integration engine, the redb.Tsak host for modules and the redb.Identity login server. Data is a C# class, a process is a route, an external system is an address string. Every client gets the same project structure. A project starts from a template. items.title: Why Website Blockers Didn't Work for Me — So I Built an Internet Off-Switch for Mac
items.summary: I tried every website blocker I could find on Mac. Browser extensions. Blocklists. Screen Time. Paid focus apps. They all worked for about two days. Then my brain found a way around them: Blocked YouTube in Chrome? I opened Safari. Blocked Twitter and Reddit? I started checking Hacker News, email, Slack, or random docs. Put a password on Screen Time? I clicked "Ignore Limit" without even thinking. Got annoyed at a browser extension? Two clicks and it was off. The problem was never my list of blocked sites. The problem was that as long as my Mac was online, there was always another tab to open. I did not want to maintain a list of 50 websites. I did not want a browser extension reading every URL I visit. And I did not want a monthly subscription just to focus. I wanted one button: turn off the internet on my Mac for 1 hour, and do not let me undo it on impulse. Just unplugging Wi-Fi does not work either — turning Wi-Fi back on takes half a second, and it happens on autopilot before you even realize you did it. So I built Vow. items.summary: Hi! I have been a .NET developer since 2016, mostly on the backend, and an open source contributor since 2019. Most of my work is about data: moving it, storing it and reading it back. You make sure that a record on one side becomes exactly the same record on the other side. Every field, every value. And then a date shows up. A date does not look suspicious. CreatedAt on every record in the database and the job is done. It behaves perfectly well until two users open the same screen in two different time zones. Then the same row says Sunday to one of them and Monday to the other. And the worst part: both of them are right. Some time ago we had a UI used by people from different time zones. One of its main features was filtering the data by date. The app had a DateTimeOffset, but the column in SQL Server was datetime2. SQL Server copies the date and the time and cuts the offset off, so 01:30+02:00 became just 01:30. People got different results depending on the time zone they ran the query from. items.title: React Hook Form for Beginners: Forms That Don't Re-Render on Every Keystroke
items.summary: Forms are where React apps quietly get slow. The classic approach stores every keystroke in state, which re-renders the whole form on every character typed. React Hook Form takes a different path: it reads values from uncontrolled inputs, so your component barely re-renders at all. Getting started takes minutes: import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form'; function SignupForm() { const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm(); const onSubmit = (data) => console.log(data); return ( {errors.email && {errors.email.message} } {errors.password && Password must be at least 8 characters. } Sign up ); } The register function connects each input to the form. Validation rules like required and minLength live right next to the field, and errors appear in formState.errors without any extra code. This approach has two big wins. First, performance: typing in one field does not re-render the others, which matters a lot in long forms. Second, less code: no value and onChange handler for every single input. items.title: SWR for Beginners: Data Fetching in React Without the Boilerplate
items.summary: Fetching data in React used to mean writing the same useEffect + useState + loading flag in every component. SWR, built by the Vercel team, replaces all of that with one hook — and adds caching, revalidation, and error handling for free. The name comes from "stale-while-revalidate": SWR shows you the cached data immediately, then quietly fetches fresh data in the background and updates the UI. Your app feels instant even on a slow network. Here is the whole idea in a few lines: import useSWR from 'swr'; const fetcher = (url) => fetch(url).then((res) => res.json()); function UserProfile({ id }) { const { data, error, isLoading } = useSWR(`/api/users/${id}`, fetcher); if (isLoading) return Loading... ; if (error) return Something went wrong. ; return {data.name} ; } That is it. No manual loading state, no effect cleanup, no duplicate requests. If two components ask for the same URL, SWR makes one request and shares the result. items.title: Building a snippet keyboard for iPhone and a paste picker for the Mac menu bar
items.summary: I make Cutling, an app that keeps the text you type again and again (your address, bank details, an email signature, the reply you send every week) and pastes it with one tap. On iPhone and iPad it's a keyboard you switch to in any app; on the Mac it sits in the menu bar and Shift-Command-V opens a picker at your cursor. The code is open source under GPL-3.0 (GitHub). Here's how the two halves work, and the platform corners I ran into. A custom keyboard gets a textDocumentProxy, and inserting a snippet is one call: proxy.insertText(value). Images are different, because a keyboard can't insert an image into a text field. Cutling puts the image on UIPasteboard.general with its real type (it reads the type from the data with CGImageSourceGetType, so a GIF stays a GIF) and you paste it. That pasteboard write is why the keyboard asks for Full Access (RequestsOpenAccess in its Info.plist). Without it, a keyboard extension can't touch the pasteboard or the shared container at all. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. items.title: Azure Functions Integration Tests with Testcontainers and Azurite
items.summary: Which bugs in a queue-triggered Azure Function can a test with a mocked QueueClient never catch? Every bug that lives in the storage service or in the trigger binding instead of in your code: the encoding of the queue message, a blob container that doesn't exist yet, the naming rules for containers and blobs, and the JSON the worker has to deserialize. A test against a real Azurite container catches all four. With one container for the whole test run, the sample's six tests, two of them through a running Functions host, finish in under ten seconds on my machine. The unit testing article from earlier this year is the baseline: business logic in a service class, the function class tested with fakes, and a first look at Testcontainers. This series picks up where it stopped. Part 1 stays with Azure Storage, queues in and blobs out; the later parts cover Cosmos DB, Service Bus, architecture rules, contracts, load and CI. The code is in the companion repo, on .NET 10 with the isolated worker, xUnit v3 and Testcontainers 4.16. The repo moved to those versions after the unit testing article, so that article's code no longer matches it line for line. An API puts orders on the orders queue.

The gateway had delivered the status report successfully. The report itself said that a simulated service was down. That response captured the design question behind OpsPulse, an incident-management API I built with ASP.NET Core. items.summary: Most teens now talk to AI chatbots every day. Pew Research found in early 2026 that about 64% of US teens use them, and roughly 3 in 10 use them daily. Only about half of parents think their teen uses them at all. We're building TeenCue, parental controls for AI. The idea is simple: let a parent know when one of their kid's AI chats may need a closer look, by topic and concern level, without ever showing the parent what was typed. On a computer that's a browser extension problem. On an iPhone it's much harder, and this post is about how we approached it. On iOS, third-party apps are sandboxed. There is no supported way for one app to read what happens inside another app, and that's a good thing. It also means a parental controls app can't see what a teen types into the ChatGPT, Gemini or Character AI apps. The usual workarounds are heavy: VPNs that route all traffic through a server Configuration profiles or MDM that take over the device Reading everything, which turns parental controls into surveillance We didn't want any of those. items.title: Offline reverse geocoding on iPhone with one memory-mapped file
items.summary: Disclosure: I work on ClearWhirl, an iPhone app that works out what is in your photo library on the device, with no upload. Places is one of its features. Every photo with a location carries a latitude and longitude. Turning that into "Lisbon, Portugal" normally means CLGeocoder, which sends the coordinates to Apple's servers and is rate limited. For an app whose promise is that your library never leaves the phone, and which has to do it for thousands of photos, that was a non-starter. We replaced it with one bundled binary file, memory-mapped, and plain geometry. This is how it works. PHAsset.location is metadata. No new permission is needed beyond the photo library access you already have, and no pixel is read. That is the first privacy win: you are using data the library already holds. What you do with the coordinates then decides whether it stays private. Regions: Natural Earth 1:10m admin-1 borders (public domain), simplified to about 330 m so the file stays small. Cities: GeoNames cities5000 (CC BY 4.0) for names and IANA time zones. Credit it in your app. We have an Acknowledgements screen. A Python build script packs both into places.bin, about 4.3 MB. The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works. This is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems. The hope is that the harsh vacuum of the cosmos will be a better fit for the technology. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Xcode Instruments in Practice: Profiling and Optimizing iOS Apps
items.summary: Most performance bugs I've chased in production iOS apps didn't come from code that was obviously slow. They came from code that was fine with test data and fell over with real data. Think of a list that scrolls smoothly with 20 items and stutters with 2,000, or a screen that opens instantly on a new iPhone and takes a second on a three-year-old one. A sort that runs on the main thread "because it's fast", until someone's account has eight years of history. You can't find these by reading code. You find them by measuring. Xcode Instruments is the tool Apple gives us for that. This article walks through the workflow I use: profile, investigate, optimize, verify. It uses real Swift 6 code and the Instruments features in current Xcode releases. The usual symptoms we're hunting: Slow screen transitions, where a push or sheet animates late or stutters. UI freezes, where the main thread is busy or blocked and taps don't register. High CPU use that drains battery and heats the device. Excessive memory allocations that cause churn, peak-memory spikes, and terminations. SwiftUI view bodies re-evaluating far more often than the data changes. Someone picked eighty pictures, the app processed forty, hit a file that wouldn't decode, and handed back nothing. Or worse: it left a half-written JPEG in Recents and no explanation of what happened. I build BatchMark, an iPhone app for finishing photos in batches. When a set is being watermarked or filtered, the export has to finish the photos it can, skip the ones it can't, and leave the phone no messier than it was before. This post is a teaching extract of that job structure, not the app's source. The image processing itself is out of scope. What matters here is how you run the job. The shape I keep coming back to has four parts: Treat each photo as its own unit of work, with its own result. Write to a temporary file first, and only move it when the write has finished. Keep going after a failure, and collect the errors. Honour cancellation between photos, and clean up anything you created. items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released! (11 minute read)
items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 simplifies both administration and development for mission-critical workloads at scale. The release introduces the `REPACK (CONCURRENTLY)` command, which enables users to optimize tables for their current workload without disruption to ongoing operations. It also gives users better control over plan stability and query performance with the new pg_plan_advice extension. PostgreSQL 19 gives users new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and build applications that span multiple systems.

items.title: The AI Forecasting Agenda (21 minute read)
items.summary: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. Researchers now need to study how this success decays as the technology is applied to different types of non-traditional forecasting questions. This post looks at how AI performs in other types of forecasting.

items.title: Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding (4 minute read)
items.summary: Apple is developing an autonomous AI agent that can get things done on behalf of users similar to offerings by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others. The company is currently seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant that can write code, browse the web, control apps, and navigate devices on a user's behalf. Apple is working on agents that can plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs while coordinating specialized subagents along the way. The company's App Store has been dominated by AI agents, so it has introduced a new warning in the upcoming macOS 27.3 update that prompts users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

items.title: AI is already massively speeding up AI research (9 minute read)
items.summary: AI companies are not ready to handle the risks of recursive self-improvement safely and responsibly, despite having talked about them for years, and this is incredibly dangerous. Policymakers need to make it a top priority to rapidly understand these risks, and consider pausing or pacing frontier AI progress. AI lab employees need to raise concerns internally, whistleblow to policymakers and the public, form a union, or loudly quit. Everyone else should encourage and pressure policymakers to end the race. Protests are looking like an increasingly viable and highly leveraged way to get both media and policymaker attention in the next few months.

items.title: What three months of shipping an AlarmKit app taught me
items.summary: In late August we shipped a small iOS 26 app that turns calendar events into AlarmKit alarms: if an event title contains a keyword you registered, a real alarm rings some minutes before it, through Silent mode and Focus, until you stop it. I wrote up the launch-week lessons back then. This post is the other half: things that only showed up after real people had been using it for a few months. None of them are in the docs, and one of them came from a user report that ended with "I had to restart my phone". AlarmPresentation.Alert takes LocalizedStringResource values for the title and buttons. It is tempting to pass keys and let the system localize them. The full-screen alert is rendered by a system process, not by your app. When that process resolves a LocalizedStringResource, "the main bundle" is not your app. In our case the alarm came up showing the raw key — in our project the source language is Japanese, so English users saw Japanese. Other developers have reported the same thing after a device restart (FB20472264 on the Apple Developer Forums). items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone.
